transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-16 | 14:00 PST | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Grace Lin (Head of ML, Helix), Samir Patel (Infra Lead, Helix), Olivia Zhou (VP Eng, Helix)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, really appreciate you taking the time. Quick intros — I'm Maya, I'm the AE working with finance and infra teams, and Diego's our solutions engineer.
[00:07] Diego: Hi all. Diego Ramos, SE, I focus on latency/throughput and pilot setups.
[00:11] Grace: Hi, Grace Lin. I run ML at Helix.
[00:13] Samir: Samir Patel — infra.
[00:15] Olivia: Olivia Zhou — VP Eng, overlapping with infra and platform.
[00:18] Maya: Cool, goal for today — dig into cost/unit economics for Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private, understand your traffic profile and constraints, and figure out a pilot. Grace, do you want to kick off with how you're using LLMs today?
[00:30] Grace: Yeah sure. So we're running a bunch of models for research and for product features — document summarization for our investor docs and an assistant that drafts emails. Right now prod uses a combination of OpenAI hosted for rapid iteration and some on-prem weights for inference for sensitive data. Typical request size is like 300 to 800 tokens input, response 150 to 400 tokens. Peak QPS around 8 req/s but most of the day it's 1 to 2 req/s. Monthly token volume maybe 250M to 400M tokens — that's our rough target.
[01:05] Diego: Got it. And when you say on-prem weights, are those a small fleet you run for some customers, or internal research only?
[01:12] Grace: Internal research and a handful of enterprise clients with strict residency needs. The on-prem stuff is for PII-sensitive workflows.
[01:19] Maya: That matches what we've seen — hybrid patterns are common. Can you share the cost target or budget constraints? What would be the threshold for hosted vs dedicated?
[01:30] Olivia: We're trying to keep monthly inference spend under $40k initially. If we go to dedicated capacity it has a baseline reserved monthly cost, so we need to see the unit math.
[01:41] Samir: Also we care about 99th pctl latency under 250ms for short chat prompts, and a hard requirement of SOC2 and KMS integration for keys.
[01:52] Diego: Cool. Couple of places where cost moves: raw per-token price, batching and throughput efficiency, and caching (prefix/KV). For hosted we have per-token pricing that varies by model family — as a ballpark, smaller open models are priced lower, larger higher. For dedicated you trade a monthly committed cost for much lower marginal cost per token. Caching and batching can reduce effective token spend a lot depending on workload.
[02:13] Grace: Can you quantify batching impact? Our patterns are pretty bursty and also we have sax of small prompts for the assistant.
[02:20] Diego: Sure. If you can batch across concurrent requests — e.g., multiple user prompts that arrive within the batching window — you amortize some of the attention compute. Effective per-token compute cost can go down 10–50% depending on batch sizes. With continuous batching in our runtime, for a high QPS steady workload you typically see 25–40% improvement. For bursty low-QPS workloads the gains are smaller unless you accept slightly higher latency.
[02:46] Samir: Hmm, we can't add 50–100ms extra on p99, so batching windows are tricky.
[02:51] Diego: Right, we tune per-route SLOs. For your 250ms p99 goal we can keep batching windows tiny and instead rely more on prefix/KV caching. If a lot of your assistant requests share the same prefix (like conversation history or templates) we can cache KV states and avoid re-encoding tokens. For long-lived convs caching has reduced token re-compute by 30–70% in similar customers.
[03:16] Grace: That's interesting — for our summarization flows there's a lot of shared context; drafts often start with standard prompt templates.
[03:22] Maya: So two levers: batching for throughput/burst, caching for repeated prefixes. The other dimension is model size/quality — smaller models lower cost but might not match quality for investor-summary use case.
[03:33] Olivia: What does a cost comparison look like numerically? Ballpark hosted per-token vs dedicated marginal cost?
[03:39] Diego: Broadly: hosted per 1k tokens for mid-size open models might be, ballpark, $0.5–$2.5 per 1k tokens depending on model and context length — sorry that's a wide range, but the key is dedicated can reduce marginal compute cost by ~40–70% once you're amortizing the reserved instance. I can share a spreadsheet we use to model this. The important inputs are monthly token volume, average prompt+response tokens, request concurrency, and acceptable latency SLOs.
[04:10] Samir: That hosted range seems high to me — is that including our use case with large responses?
[04:15] Diego: Yeah included end-to-end. I'll follow up with a clearer hosted vs dedicated sheet with examples using your token sizes.
[04:21] Grace: Can you explain how cache hit rate translates to token savings? If we get 50% cache hit on prefix tokens what's the math?
[04:29] Diego: Simple example: if input is 600 tokens and response 300 tokens, total 900 tokens. If 300 of those are prefix tokens that are cached and you have 50% hit, you save 150 input tokens per request. So effective tokens go from 900 to 750, that's ~17% reduction in token spend. If cache hits are higher on repeated prompts it quickly compounds.
[04:53] Olivia: For the assistant we see a lot of repeated system prompt material and templates, so I could see 40–60% cacheable in steady state.
[05:02] Maya: One nuance — caching interacts with model variant and quantization. On dedicated you can run quantized variants which cut inference cost further, but you need to validate quality. We often recommend a small A/B to ensure no regression.
[05:16] Grace: Right. On that note, for our regulated customers we might need VPC/private deployment. How does that change the unit economics?
[05:24] Diego: Private deployments add infra and ops costs — typically a larger upfront and per-month platform fee vs hosted. The marginal per-token compute cost can still be competitive if you run on dedicated hardware and do quantization, but you take on more responsibility. For customers with strict residency or audit needs, private makes sense but it moves you from pure unit economics to TCO analysis (hardware, networking, ops).
[05:46] Samir: For private, we need KMS/HSM integration, no egress to 3rd party, and audit logs stored for 1 year. Is that supported?
[05:55] Diego: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS integrations and configurable audit log retention. We'll share the SOC2 whitepaper and the infra checklist.
[06:03] Grace: Great. What about burst capacity? We have occasional high-volume marketing blasts where QPS spikes x10 for 15 minutes.
[06:10] Diego: For dedicated you can configure burst policies — keep a buffer of burstable capacity or allow routing to hosted as overflow. Cost tradeoff: reserved plus burst buffer vs paying hosted marginal rate during spikes. Some customers combine both: dedicated for baseline and hosted overflow for unpredictable spikes.
[06:27] Olivia: Hmm, how is overflow routed? Latency and data residency concerns may block routing sensitive requests to hosted.
[06:34] Maya: Routing is policy-driven: route by region, model compatibility, or tag (sensitive). We can set rules to never route sensitive tagged requests off private/dedicated. Non-sensitive can go to hosted during spikes.
[06:45] Grace: That helps. Back to numbers — if we model 300M tokens/month with 40% caching plus batching gains 25%, do you have a sample calculation?
[06:55] Diego: Rough quick calc: start 300M raw tokens. Caching 40% saves 120M, so effective 180M. Batching/throughput efficiency 25% reduces compute equivalent to another 45M, so effective ~135M tokens billed. Then multiply by per-token rate — for dedicated marginal maybe $0.5 per 1k tokens in this hypothetical — 135M tokens / 1k = 135k * $0.5 = $67.5k/month. Hosted could be 2x that in our broad ranges depending on model. I'll put numbers into the spreadsheet with model families and quantization tiers so you can see break-even for reserved cost.
[07:39] Samir: Okay that math makes sense as a raw approach. Our target budget earlier was $40k/mo, so we need to see if we can get to that with quantization and smaller models for some flows.
[07:49] Diego: Exactly, you can mix model families. Use a smaller quantized model for assistant conversation and larger model for summarization. Redwood's routing supports per-route model mapping, and the console gives token-level cost breakdown so you can see spend per feature.
[08:03] Olivia: How long is a dedicated commit/contract typically? 6/12 months?
[08:07] Maya: Typically annual for best pricing, but we do 6-month pilots for some customers. It depends on how quickly you can prove steady-state usage. For pilots we can do a short-term reserved or a burst-from-hosted plan with a projected commit based on benchmark results.
[08:21] Grace: For the benchmark, what do you need from us?
[08:24] Diego: A sample traffic trace or distribution: average tokens per request, percentile lengths, concurrency distribution and a set of prompt templates. Samir can provide a one-week trace anonymized. We'll run a benchmark across hosted and dedicated (or equivalent sim) and show p50/p95/p99 and effective token cost after batching/caching.
[08:40] Samir: We can give that. We'll need details on endpoints and a security PO to sign before any test with real data.
[08:48] Maya: We can do synthetic data runs first. For any real data we follow a security onboarding — Diego will send the infra checklist.
[08:55] Grace: Also curious about evals and quality monitoring — if we switch models or quantize, can we get regression alerts on quality?
[09:01] Diego: Yes, Redwood Optimize integrates quality monitoring tied to prompt sets/evals and will alert if you hit regression thresholds. We can set that up as part of the pilot.
[09:10] Olivia: Competitors question — we currently run some flows on OpenAI and are evaluating Anthropic too. How do you compare on cost?
[09:17] Maya: High level: open-model hosting like ours is often more cost-competitive than closed-model hosted providers at scale, especially if you go dedicated. We'll put together a competitive appendix in the pricing deck.
[09:29] Grace: Sounds good. Any security artifact links you can send now?
[09:32] Diego: I'll email the SOC2 + KMS + private deployment checklist after the call. Link to whitepaper: (sent in chat) https://redwood.example/whitepaper-soc2 (note: placeholder).
[09:43] Maya: Ok quick recap and next steps: 1) Maya send hosted vs dedicated pricing sheet + unit econ model by Wed 3/18. 2) Diego send SOC2/security whitepaper and infra checklist by Tue 3/17. 3) Samir provide traffic profile by Fri 3/20. 4) Schedule technical benchmark with Samir/Diego the week of 3/23. Any other items?
[10:03] Grace: No that's good. We'll look at the math and meet again after the benchmark.
[10:07] Olivia: Thank you.
[10:09] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with assets.

End of transcript (approx 45m). Notes: occasional transcription noise; speaker turns approximate.
